newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU farmers, governments rap Commission reform plan.
newsitem.headline: EU farmers, governments rap Commission reform plan.

text.p: A European Commission plan for price-cutting farm reforms to prepare for the European Union's eastern enlargement ran into a predictable barrage of criticism from west European farmers and some governments on Wednesday.

In France and Germany, whose big grain barons the Brussels executive accuses of hogging European subsidies, farmers' leaders declared the proposals unacceptable and vowed to fight any dismantling of the EU Common Agricultural Policy (CAP).

"These proposals are still not acceptable as they stand," thundered France's main FNSEA farm union, which fought a bitter battle in defence of production subsidies and against compulsory farmland set-asides during the 1993 GATT world trade talks.
"(The EU) must not follow the logic of pure accountancy which would lead to a dismantling of the CAP," it said.

The French government said the Agenda 2000 plan, which aims to make European farmers more competitive by lowering prices towards world levels, would weaken rather than boost the EU's bargaining position in the next World Trade Organisation (WTO) negotiations.

The Commission proposal to shift agriculture support from guaranteed prices and export subsidies to direct payments to farmers might also prove costly and disadvantage some farm sectors, French Agriculture Minister Louis Le Pensec said.
At present about 80 percent of EU farm subsidies go to just 20 percent of farmers.

European Commission President Jacques Santer unveiled the plan on Wednesday in Strasbourg. It aims to prepare for the entry of agriculturally backward east European states early next century and prevent a return of costly EU food surpluses.

The German farmers' union (DBV), whose members are among the biggest beneficiaries of the CAP, said its producers stood to lose one fifth of their incomes from beef, grain, oilseeds and milk if the proposals were implemented.

"Strategic thinking ahead of the new world trade round and the eastward expansion of the EU is necessary. But equally important are long-term perspectives for our farmers and their participation in general income growth," DBV president Gerd Sonnleitner said in a statement.
The DBV was ready to discuss the package constructively, but it would not shy away from a confrontation if necessary.
Britain's National Farmers Union gave a qualified welcome to the plan, despite misgivings in detail, saying it "will help us achieve the all-important move towards the market place".

The Commission has estimated cereals farmers received 8.5 billion European currency units ($9.4 billion) too much over the past four years after crop failures sent world market prices soaring and cuts in EU support prices failed to bite.
Most of the money went to wealthy grain barons in northern France, Germany and eastern England.
EU agriculture ministers last month rejected a Commission proposal for even a modest cut in cereals subsidies.
Santer told the European parliament that cuts in support prices would strengthen the EU's position in the next round of global WTO farm negotiations due to start in 1999.

But Le Pensec said that voluntary prices cuts ahead of talks might just force the EU into making further concessions to its trade partners on farm import tariffs or on the terms for access to EU markets.
"This strategy cannot be accepted as such by France and also by EU ministers," he said.

France's left-wing government remembers how the last Socialist Paris administration was hounded from office in 1993 partly by violent farmers' protests over the negotiations, said it would review the plan carefully and consult farm organisations before taking a position.
Finland also expressed concern at the Commission proposals, saying they overlooked the tough economics of farming in a harsh climate.
"The commission proposal for a decrease in the price of grain is problematic from Finland's point of view," the agriculture ministry said in a statement.
